To understand the three kinds of keigo: ていねいご (です/ます), そんけいご (you raise the other person) and けんじょうご (you lower yourself, ch. 37).
To use the special respectful verbs: いらっしゃる, めしあがる, おっしゃる, ごらんに なる, なさる, ごぞんじ, くださる, おやすみに なる.

The last Monday in November, nine in the morning, at the entrance of the hospital in Bucharest. Mr Tanaka is visiting: he is the president of the Japanese company ひかり メディカル (Hikari Medical), which makes medical equipment, and the hospital wants to buy a new machine from them for the department. Dr Ionescu found out that Mihai is learning Japanese and asked him to welcome the guest. Ionescu speaks Romanian (here his lines are written in simple, everyday Japanese); Mihai passes them on in polite Japanese.
Mr Tanaka, welcome. I’m Mihai, a doctor here. Pleased to meet you.
(Handing him his business card) Tanaka, from Hikari Medical. Oh, your Japanese is excellent.
No, I still have a lot to learn. When did you arrive in Bucharest, sir?
Last night. The plane from Vienna was delayed, so I only got to the hotel at midnight.
That must have been tiring. Did you sleep well last night?
Yes, thank you. This morning I even took a little walk around the hotel.
(In Romanian) Mihai, offer Mr Tanaka a coffee.
Sir, would you like a coffee?
Thank you, I’d love one. …Is the gentleman over there Dr Ionescu?
Yes, that’s my boss, Ionescu. He speaks English too.
(After greeting him in English) Where is the machine you’re using now?
On the third floor. The lift is this way.
By the way, Mr Mihai, where did you learn Japanese?
(wrong) In Madrid, I “deigned” to study on my own.
(Laughing) Mr Mihai, “o-… ni naru” isn’t used about yourself. It’s a word for the other person.
Oh, I’m sorry! I studied on my own.
Never mind. When I was young, I made lots of mistakes in English too, in America.
This is the current machine. It’s from Hikari Medical, a machine from fifteen years ago.
What memories! It’s the machine from the year I left medicine and joined the company.
What? You were a doctor, sir?
Yes, long ago. So today let’s talk doctor to doctor.
(In Romanian) Mihai, tell him we’re having lunch together.
Sir, how about lunch together with Dr Ionescu? Do you know sarmale, the Romanian dish?
Sarmale? No, I don’t know them. But since I’m here, I’d like to try them.

me-shi-a-ga-ru: five even syllables, with no stressed syllable as in English. “shi” is short, almost whispered: me-sh(i)-a-ga-ru.
go-ran-ni na-ru: ん links to に, but it lasts a whole syllable: go-ra-n-ni. The same goes for おやすみに, おつきに: don’t swallow the “ni”.
1. What keigo is: three kinds of politeness

So far you’ve spoken politely with です / ます. This is called ていねいご (neutral polite language): it’s polite without changing the verb itself. Japanese, however, has two more levels, used with customers, guests, bosses, teachers and older people you don’t know well. All of it together is called けいご (keigo).
RAISES the person doing the action
Think of a staircase: to show respect, you either lift the other person up (そんけいご) or step down yourself (けんじょうご). Either way the distance between you grows, and in Japanese that means respect.

English shows politeness mostly with set phrases and indirectness: “Would you like…?”, “sir”, “madam”. Only rarely do we use special verbs: “to deign”, “to partake” (“will you partake?”), “His Majesty”. In Japanese, politeness sits right in the VERB: the same “to eat” becomes a different word (めしあがる) when you talk about a guest.
You’ve already met keigo without knowing it: いらっしゃいませ (welcome, in a shop, ch. 11), いらっしゃいます (is, about a person, ch. 14), ようこそ いらっしゃいました (ch. 17), もうします (my name is, ch. 14; that’s けんじょうご).

The most common verbs have a completely different word for respect. You have to learn these by heart, like new words. You use them when the SUBJECT is the person you respect (the guest, the boss, the teacher).

Five verbs are irregular in ～ます: いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, なさる, くださる (and ござる) change る to い: いらっしゃいます, NOT いらっしゃります. This is also where phrases you already know come from: ください (from くださる), いらっしゃい(ませ). All their other forms are regular (godan): いらっしゃって, おっしゃった, なさらない.
When did you arrive in Bucharest, sir?
What did Dr Ionescu say? (asked by someone from outside)
いらっしゃる has three meanings (to be, to come, to go): context tells you which. いつ いらっしゃいました か = when did you come?; どちら へ いらっしゃいます か = where are you going?; せんせい は いらっしゃいます か = is the doctor in?
3. The regular form: お + stem + に なる
For most other verbs there’s a recipe: お + stem (the ～ます form without ます) + に なる. Literally: “the gentleman becomes (the one who) waits”. It sounds more indirect, and so more respectful.

Only なる is conjugated: おつきに なりました (has arrived), おかえりに なりません (isn’t going back), おまちに なって います (is waiting for you / is waiting). With “Sino-Japanese noun + する” verbs you use ご instead of お: にゅういん する (to be admitted to hospital) → ごにゅういん に なる; りよう する (to use a service) → ごりよう に なる. A few very common words still take お (おべんきょう, おでんわ), but with them, about someone else, べんきょう なさる or べんきょう される is more natural.
Mr Tanaka is going back to the hotel at four.
Would you like to use this pen?

The recipe does NOT work when the stem has only one syllable: みる → み, ねる → ね, いる → い, くる → き, する → し. There’s no *おみに なる or *おしに なる: for these you use the special verbs (ごらんに なる, おやすみに なる, いらっしゃる, なさる). And if a verb has a special form, prefer that one: おたべに なる exists, but めしあがる is much more natural.
4. The third way: the passive as respect
Remember the passive from ch. 31 (かかれる, こられる, される)? The same form can also express respect, a lighter, more “office-style” kind. It’s very common at work, in the news and among senior colleagues.
The levels of respect, from simplest to highest: かえります → かえられます → おかえりに なります. With a very important guest (a customer, a company president) you choose the special verb or お～に なる.

Watch out for confusion: たべられます can be passive (“is eaten”), potential (“can eat”) or respectful (“eats”, about someone important). Only context decides. That’s why, to be clear, with guests people say めしあがります.
5. When NOT to use 尊敬語

The golden rule: 尊敬語 describes the OTHER person’s actions. Never your own. If you say おべんきょう に なりました about yourself, it’s like saying in English “I deigned to study”: it sounds comic or arrogant. That’s exactly Mihai’s mistake in the dialogue.

Don’t repeat the respectful form when you ANSWER, either. If you’re asked “サルマレ を ごぞんじ です か”, you answer はい、しって います or いいえ、しりません (or, very humbly, ぞんじません — ch. 37). To “コーヒー を めしあがります か” you answer はい、いただきます.

Respect also goes on NOUNS, for the other person’s things: お/ご + noun. おなまえ (your name), ごかぞく (your family), おしごと (your job), おくさま (your wife), but about your own: つま (my wife). And ～さま is more respectful than ～さん: おきゃくさま, おいしゃさま. A job title takes the place of “Mr”: たなかしゃちょう, イオネスクせんせい.

Did you notice that Mihai, talking to Mr Tanaka, calls his boss just イオネスク, without “-san”? In Japanese, when you talk to someone from OUTSIDE (a customer, a guest), the people in your own group (family, colleagues, even your boss) aren’t “raised”. More on this, and on humble language, in chapter 37.

ポケット の カード — The card in the pocket
On Saturday afternoon, as usual, Ioana came over to practise Japanese.
Mihai said, looking a bit worried: “On Monday the president of a Japanese company is coming to the hospital. And they asked me to show him around.”
“Great! Then let’s practise keigo. I’ll play the director.”
Ioana sat down on the sofa, straightened her back and put on a stern face.
Mihai cleared his throat and began: “Sir, will you eat a coffee?”
“Wrong! Coffee is something you drink. And to a director you say ‘meshiagarimasu ka’.”
Ana’s laughter came from the kitchen.
“OK, once more. Sir, did you come to Bucharest yesterday?” “‘Irasshaimashita ka’!”
“Ah, yes, yes. …I was just about to ‘deign to say’ that myself.”
This time both Ana and Ioana doubled up with laughter. “You don’t use ‘ossharu’ about yourself!”
Mihai tried once more. “Sir, would you like to see this photo?”
“Yes, very good.” Ioana nodded like a teacher.
“Sir, what are you planning to do in Bucharest?” “I’d like to eat good food.” “Then please be sure to try sarmale.”
As she was leaving, Ioana laughed at the door: “Good luck on Monday! I’d have liked to meet the director too.”
That evening, Mihai wrote the words on a small card. “To be, to go, to come” → irassharu. “To eat, to drink” → meshiagaru. “To say” → ossharu. “To see” → goran ni naru.
Then he put the card in the pocket of his white coat, ready in advance.
On Monday, Mr Tanaka turned out to be a quiet and very kind man.
After the morning coffee, they looked at the old machine on the third floor.
As he walked around the hospital, the director noted down everything in a little notebook.
Before answering questions, Mihai now and then sneaked a look at the card in his pocket.
The third time, the director noticed. “Mr Mihai, what’s that card?”
Mihai went red, but honestly showed him the card.
The director read the card and laughed, clearly pleased. “My granddaughter is making exactly the same card at school.”
“You have a granddaughter?” “Yes, an eleven-year-old girl. She’s not very good at keigo.”
At lunch they ate sarmale at a small restaurant near the hospital.
The director ate one and his eyes went wide. “These are delicious! They’re like the cabbage rolls we have in Japan.”
When Mihai asked “Would you like another one?”, the director said “Well, I won’t say no” and in the end ate three.
Mihai thought to himself: “If they were Mrs Doina’s sarmale, he’d surely eat five.”
During the meal, the director asked Mihai about his family. “What does your wife do in Bucharest?”
“My wife teaches Spanish. She’s pregnant now: a little girl is due in January.”
“Congratulations!” The director was as happy as if it were his own news.
“Then on Wednesday evening let’s have dinner together with Dr Ionescu. And your wife too, by all means.”
As they left, the director said “gochisōsama deshita” to the waiter, in Japanese, and made everyone laugh.
At two in the afternoon, the director talked to the young doctors about the new machine.
The director spoke in English, but he said the difficult parts in Japanese, and Mihai translated them into Romanian.
At the end, one of the young doctors asked a question. Mihai thought for a moment and translated it politely: “Sir, why did you give up being a doctor?”
The director answered quietly: “A doctor helps the patient in front of him. A good machine helps patients all over the world. That’s why.”
The room was silent for a moment, then everyone applauded.
Later, Mihai was praised by Dr Ionescu (“Your translating today was very good”) and felt a little embarrassed.
At four in the afternoon, before they parted, the director took a thin book out of his bag. It was a keigo book for children.
“I bought it for my granddaughter, but I’m giving it to you. I’ll buy her another one.”
“Thank you from the bottom of my heart for giving me something so precious.” Mihai bowed deeply.
That evening, as soon as he got home, Mihai collapsed on the sofa.
“All day long my head was full of ‘irassharu’ and ‘meshiagaru’.”
Ana brought him a warm tea and laughed. “You worked hard today. Doctor, would you care for some tea?”
“Stop it.” Mihai laughed too and drank the tea.
“So, what’s Mr Tanaka like?” Ana asked.
“A man whose face is happiest when he talks about his granddaughter. You’ll like him too, I’m sure.”
“I’m coming on Wednesday too, right? I’m a bit nervous.”
Then he opened the book he’d been given by the director. On the first page it said:
“Words that raise the other person and words that lower yourself. Keigo has two paths.”
Mihai turned the page and sighed. “Words that lower yourself… I have to learn these too by Wednesday.”
Ana patted him on the shoulder. “Don’t worry. This time I’ll work hard with you.”
Just then, in her tummy, the baby kicked too.
